sentences.text: Hatzegopteryx is an extinct genus of azhdarchid pterosaur known from incomplete remains found in Transylvania, Romania.
The largest bones suggest a wingspan ranging from 10 to 12 meters, ranking it among the largest flying reptiles.
In contrast, a medium-sized shoulder bone found in the Sânpetru Formation likely belonged to an individual with a wingspan of 4.5 to 5 meters.
The skull was broadened in the rear, measuring 0.5 meters wide across the quadrate bones.
This animal apparently possessed a robust skull expanded at the back and an enormous jaw.
The posterior neck vertebrae could withstand between five and ten times the animal's body weight.
The genus Hatzegopteryx was named by Buffetaut and colleagues in 2002.
The first remains were found in the upper part of the Densuș Ciula Formation in Vălioara, Romania, dated to the Late Maastrichtian about 66 million years ago.
A single large neck vertebra known as the RR specimen or EME 215 was found at the Râpa Roșie locality of the Sebeș Formation.
Hatzegopteryx was likely a terrestrial generalist predator, similar to other azhdarchid pterosaurs.
It likely fed on animals that lived on the ground.
Its robust anatomy suggests it could prey on animals too large to swallow whole, unlike other giant azhdarchids.
Researchers suggest Hatzegopteryx acted as an apex predator in the Hațeg Island ecosystem due to its large size.
In the absence of large theropods, it was likely the apex predator of the Hațeg Island ecosystem during the Late Cretaceous, hunting prey proportionally larger than other azhdarchids.
Despite its unusually large and robust skull, Hatzegopteryx was not flightless, as its wing bones resemble those of other flying pterosaurs.
The generic name is derived from the Hatzeg basin of Transylvania and the Greek word pteryx meaning wing.
The specific name thambema is derived from the Greek word thambema meaning terror, monster, referencing its huge size.
The parent group of Hatzegopteryx is Azhdarchidae.
In 2018, a phylogenetic analysis placed Hatzegopteryx in an advanced position within the family Azhdarchidae.
Hatzegopteryx lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
It lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Hatzegopteryx lived on the Tisia–Dacia Block, an island landmass that included the Hațeg Basin.
The island habitat of Hatzegopteryx had a subtropical climate with an average temperature of about 25°C.
It is debated whether the RR specimen belongs to Hatzegopteryx thambema due to a lack of overlapping elements, though its bone structure warrants referral to at least H. sp.
It is debated whether similarities between Hatzegopteryx and Quetzalcoatlus northropi indicate synonymy, as the humerus is considered non-diagnostic for giant azhdarchids.

In their 2002 description, Buffetaut and colleagues suggested the skull weight must have been reduced in an unconventional way to allow flight, though they admitted it could have been a non-flying animal, finding this unlikely due to similarities in wing bones with flying pterosaurs.
Although initially identified as a third cervical vertebra, a set of traits supports its identification as a vertebra from the posterior neck, specifically the seventh vertebra.
